newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Moslems fire opening shot in post-vote power fight.
newsitem.headline: Moslems fire opening shot in post-vote power fight.

text.p: Just as relieved peace sponsors were declaring Bosnia's elections by and large legitimate, the main Moslem faction cried foul and rejected the results on Serb territory before they had even been announced.

The instant challenge by President Alija Izetbegovic's SDA party was the opening thrust in a looming duel for ethnic advantage in the power-sharing system to be set up as the foundation for reunifying Bosnia.
International organisers of Saturday's elections, prescribed to resurrect a country riven into Serb, Moslem and Croat fiefs by a 1992-95 war, pronounced them widely free of violence and fraud.

They seemed unperturbed by the SDA's complaint and said it was the first of many to be expected from nationalist rivals who still instinctively resist the notion of power-sharing and, in the case of Serbs and Croats, revel in separatist rhetoric.
Officials of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) mission which supervised the elections said its appeals committee would rule on the SDA protest within 72 hours.

Western diplomats said the committee was almost certain to dismiss the complaint, leaving international peace coordinators to tackle the really hard part of the Dayton agreement -- coaxing the factions to govern together.
"The election was an essential precursor to moving into this phase of implementation," Richard Holbrooke, American architect of the Bosnian peace treaty, told CNN television.
"The SDA letter was clearly written before the election and is very generic in its complaint. It seems to be a positioning document for the future," Holbrooke said.
"We will not in any way excuse the occasional irregularities that occurred but they are not significant enough to annul the elections," a European diplomat said.
"The SDA's action was merely the opening shot of a post- election scramble. It may be just a way of mollifying Moslem hardliners in the party. We don't think there's any boycott threat," he added.
"I don't think anyone in the know is really worrying about this," said a U.S. diplomat. "It would hardly be in the interest of Izetbegovic's government to (cripple) the Dayton process now."

Holbrooke, in a pointed reminder to the SDA, said Bosnian Serb leader Biljana Plavsic had expressly promised in talks with him on Saturday that her party's nominee would join a new three- person collective presidency after the election.

He said that was an important Serb turnaround from weeks of blatantly secessionist rhetoric on the campaign trail conjuring up visions of unifying the half of Bosnia in Serb hands with Serbia -- in defiance of Dayton's writ.

Holbrooke said the Western powers had strong economic leverage on the Bosnian Serbs to comply with the process of reintegrating Bosnia, including an "outer wall" of U.N. sanctions which remain until power-sharing is established.
